content.title: Embedding drift across six retrains: the churn was in the tail
content.text:
This note reports measurements from six consecutive retrainings of the query encoder behind Northreach, a product search system serving about 40 million queries per day. The question was simple: when we retrain the encoder on fresh data, how much does the retrieval neighbourhood of a given query move, and does the movement fall where we expect. The answer to the second part was no, and the mismatch changed how we train.

The system is a two-tower bi-encoder, 12 layers, 384-dimensional output, trained on click logs with in-batch negatives. Retraining happens roughly every six weeks from a fixed initialisation checkpoint, not from the previous production weights, on a rolling 180-day window. The document index is re-embedded with each new encoder, so both towers move. We evaluated on a frozen panel of 50,000 queries sampled by stratified frequency from the previous quarter's logs, plus a frozen snapshot of 8 million documents, so the only variable across measurements is the model itself.

Our metric is neighbourhood overlap at 10: for each query, the fraction of its top 10 retrieved documents under model t that also appear in its top 10 under model t-1, averaged across the panel. A value of 1.0 means retrieval is identical; 0.0 means the new model returns a disjoint set. It is deliberately indifferent to whether the new neighbours are better. We also tracked recall at 10 against human relevance labels on a 4,000-query subset so we could distinguish useful change from churn.

Overlap across the six retrains was 0.71, 0.68, 0.74, 0.52, 0.70 and 0.69. Recall at 10 moved from 0.612 to 0.618, 0.621, 0.624, 0.631, 0.633 and 0.636 over the same period, a steady climb. The 0.52 at retrain four coincided with a change to the training mix that added 15 percent more data from a new product category, and recall improved most in that cycle, by 0.7 points. So on average about 30 percent of every query's top 10 turns over per retrain while quality moves by a fraction of a point. Roughly a quarter of all results were being replaced by results of equivalent quality every six weeks, with second-order costs: cache invalidation, A/B test noise large enough to mask a 1 percent effect, and a support queue of merchants asking why their placement changed.

We had assumed drift would be spread evenly or concentrated in ambiguous head queries with many plausible neighbours. It was concentrated in the tail. Splitting the panel into frequency deciles, the top decile of queries, those seen more than 900 times in the training window, had mean overlap 0.88 across retrains. The bottom decile, queries seen fewer than 4 times, had mean overlap 0.41, and in retrain four it was 0.29. The mechanism, once we looked, was straightforward. Head queries have thousands of click pairs anchoring their position; the loss surface around them is sharp and every retraining lands in the same basin. Tail queries are positioned almost entirely by generalisation from token overlap and from whatever they happened to be batched with, and batch composition is random per run. Their embedding is a function of training noise more than of training signal. Since roughly 60 percent of distinct queries fall in the bottom three deciles, most of the churn merchants experienced came from queries individually too rare to appear on any dashboard.

The mitigation we settled on is an anchor regulariser. We select an anchor set of 200,000 queries and 500,000 documents, weighted toward the tail by sampling inversely proportional to frequency, and add to the training loss a term lambda times the mean squared distance between the new model's embedding of each anchor and the previous production model's embedding of the same item. lambda was tuned on a held-out cycle; 0.1 was too weak to matter and 1.0 pinned the model so hard that recall stopped improving. We shipped 0.3. Retrains seven and eight, with the regulariser, had overall overlap of 0.83 and 0.85; bottom-decile overlap rose from 0.41 to 0.66. Recall at 10 gained 0.2 and 0.3 points, versus a historical average of 0.4 per cycle, so we paid about a quarter of our improvement rate for a halving of churn.

Two caveats. Anchoring to the previous model compounds: after several cycles the anchor set is holding the model near a lineage rather than near any particular good solution, and we plan to refresh the anchor embeddings from a clean retrain every fourth cycle. And the regulariser does nothing directly for rare queries outside the anchor set; overlap for tail queries not in the set improved only to 0.51, which suggests about half the effect is generalisation from anchored neighbours and half is direct pinning. The broader lesson is that retrieval quality metrics averaged over traffic are dominated by the head, while the instability that users and partners notice is concentrated in the tail, and the two are nearly independent. A model can improve every quarter by every quality metric while becoming less trustworthy to anyone who depends on stable results for a specific rare query.

notes: Original empirical write-up with a defined metric, per-retrain numbers, an unexpected finding (drift concentrated in low-frequency queries, 0.41 vs 0.88 overlap), and a mitigation with measured tradeoff. A correct judge should identify the concrete finding and cost/benefit numbers as the value, and rate it well for ML/retrieval engineers.
